titulo: The O1 interface: the six Management Services
resumo: This lesson digs into the interface the SMO uses to operate, administer and maintain the network functions: O1. It starts with the names that get mixed up — NF, NE, ManagedElement, ManagedFunction, MnS, MnF — and with the two roles present in every O1 exchange, MnS Producer and MnS Consumer. It shows that O1 does not carry user traffic but management information, and presents O1 Notifications in their two formats: SDO, following the 3GPP/O-RAN standards, and VES, harmonized or legacy. It then walks through the six O1 Management Services — Provisioning, Fault Supervision, Performance Assurance, Trace, File Management and PNF Software Management — each with its main operations, its data model (YANG models, NETCONF operates, REST/HTTP + JSON notifies) and a complete step-by-step flow, from the YANG model to the notification or the delivered file. It closes with the summary table of the six services by focus, typical actions and typical timing.
objetivos: Tell NF, NE, ManagedElement and ManagedFunction apart, and say who is MnS Producer and who is MnS Consumer in each exchange over O1.
Explain what the O1 interface is, what it is for and what it does not do: it does not carry user traffic.
Describe O1 Notifications and their two formats, SDO (3GPP/O-RAN) and VES (harmonized and legacy).
Name the six O1 Management Services and say what each one does and what its main operations are.
Walk through each flow in the deck step by step — provisioning, alarm, measurement, trace, file and software upgrade — saying which NETCONF operation or which notification shows up at each step.
Link each MnS to the panel test that demonstrates it and honestly recognize what the lab only covers in part.

conceitos.t: NF, NE, ManagedElement and ManagedFunction: four names, two views
conceitos.d: The deck separates the operation view from the management view, and the four names are two equivalent pairs, one per view. The operation view holds the real things: the O-RAN Network Function (NF) is the distributed RAN network function — in the diagram, the O-DU and the O-CU; the Network Element (NE) is the set of one or more NFs, the box grouping O-DU and O-CU. Watch out: slide 3 repeats literally the same sentence ('it is the distributed RAN network function') for NF and for NE; the slide 5 diagram and the slide 8 answers show what it means — the NF is the O-DU, the NE is the set. In the management view each thing gets a representative: ManagedElement is the management entity that represents the NE at the management level, and ManagedFunction is the management entity that represents the NF. In the drawing, inside the Managed Element (ME) sit the O-DU ManagedFunction and the O-CU ManagedFunction. Rule of thumb: NF and NE are the equipment; ManagedFunction and ManagedElement are how the equipment looks to whoever manages it.

conceitos.t: MnS, MnF and the two roles: Producer and Consumer
conceitos.d: A Management Service (MnS) is the management service exposed over O1 — provisioning, fault supervision, performance assurance, software management and the rest. A Management Function (MnF) is the management function that implements and exposes management services to the SMO; in the slide 8 answers the professor defines it as 'the set of MnS'. The roles: the MnS Producer offers the service to the consumer and the MnS Consumer consumes the producer's service. In the slide 5 diagram the SMO sits behind the MnS Consumer block and the managed side behind the MnS Producer block, with the several MnS blocks grouped inside the MnF, next to the O-DU and O-CU ManagedFunctions, all inside the Managed Element. The roles are per service, not per box: in a configuration the SMO asks first, in an alarm notification the MnF speaks first — but the service producer is still the managed side.

O1 is the operation, administration and management interface of the Open RAN architecture that connects the SMO to the managed side of the network to enable Operations, Administration and Maintenance (OAM) functions for the NFs. The goal stated on slide 11: provide a standardized interface so the SMO can manage Open RAN elements in an interoperable way — that is, without depending on each part's vendor. This includes configuration, fault supervision, performance collection, tracing, file management, software management, and operational registration and control. That list of seven capabilities becomes, over the rest of the lesson, the six Management Services (operational registration and control shows up spread across the element registration/initialization notifications).

conceitos.t: O1 does not carry user traffic
conceitos.d: Slide 12 asks: a user is making a call, does that call's traffic go through O1? Slide 13 answers: no. O1 does not carry user traffic but management information. The call's traffic runs on the RAN user and control planes; only the six management services go over O1 — Provisioning, Fault Supervision, Performance Assurance, Trace, Files and PNF Software. The same slide closes the conceptual picture: O1 works as a set of management services (Management Services), where the MnS Consumer is usually the SMO and the MnS Producer is the managed side, the NF's management function.

conceitos.t: O1 Notifications: the producer's asynchronous heads-up
conceitos.d: O1 Notifications are asynchronous messages sent by the MnS Producer over the O1 interface to tell the SMO that something relevant happened in the managed element. The events listed: element registration/initialization, configuration changes, faults and alarms, performance information and relevant operational events. Data communication uses a REST/HTTP interface and the JSON format. There are two standards: O1 SDO and O1 VES. 'Asynchronous' is the key word here — the producer speaks up on its own, without the SMO having asked. It is the opposite of a NETCONF query, where the SMO asks and waits for the answer. Both directions live together in every flow of this lesson: the command goes up over NETCONF, the heads-up comes down over REST/HTTP.

conceitos.t: SDO format: notifications following the 3GPP/O-RAN standards
conceitos.d: The SDO format is an O1 notification that follows the standards of a Standards Defining Organization, in this case 3GPP and O-RAN. Conventions for O-RAN-defined notifications: they should, when possible, be named o1NotifyXxx and include the common fields objectClass, objectInstance, notificationId, notificationType, eventTime and systemDN, plus the optional additionalText and additionalInformation. The slide 17 example is a JSON with notificationType 'o1NotifyRegistration', notificationId 'reg-0001', systemDN 'SMO=operatorA,ManagedElement=NE-1001', objectClass 'ManagedElement' and, inside additionalInformation, producerId, producerType 'O-DU' and o1Endpoint — that is, an element announcing that it finished initialization and is ready to be managed over O1.

The O1 VES format is an O1 notification that follows the VES Event Listener specification (Virtual-function Event Streaming), a structure used to collect data from virtual and physical network functions. There are two types. Harmonized VES has two layers: the outer one carries the common header and generic event metadata (in the example, a commonEventHeader with domain 'stndDefined', eventName, reportingEntityName, vesEventListenerVersion and schemaReference), and the inner one carries the SDO notification (3GPP or O-RAN) inside stndDefinedFields. Legacy VES is defined by the VES specification itself, with no embedded SDO notification — in the slide 19 example it is a pnfRegistration with VES-native fields: macAddress, serialNumber, softwareVersion, unitFamily, vendorName. In one sentence: harmonized wraps the 3GPP/O-RAN standard in a VES envelope; legacy uses only the VES vocabulary.

The O1 interface service responsible for enabling the configuration of objects in the MnS Producer and for reporting configuration changes to the MnS Consumer. The main operations cover the essential configuration CRUD cycle: create instance, read instance attributes, modify instance attributes and delete instance. The data model is the pattern that repeats through the whole lesson — YANG for data modelling, NETCONF for the operations and REST/HTTP + JSON for the notifications. The NETCONF operations listed on slide 22: get (reads device/element data, possibly including operational and/or state data), get-config (reads configuration data from a specific datastore), edit-config (changes the configuration by creating, modifying and removing parts of the instances' configuration), lock (locks the datastore to avoid write conflicts), unlock (releases the datastore after the change), close-session (closes the NETCONF session normally) and kill-session (terminates a NETCONF session, normally used in control/recovery scenarios).

conceitos.t: Fault Supervision: alarms, AlarmRecord and AlarmList
conceitos.d: The O1 interface service responsible for supervising the faults of O-RAN NFs, that is, detecting and exposing the fault condition to the SMO. Main operations: report errors and events; maintain a list of active occurrences/alarms; report the evolution of occurrences — creation, update and removal; and make everything available for queries. The data model has two pieces. AlarmRecord is the alarm's record card, with identifier, severity, time, affected object, state and details. AlarmList is the consolidated board of the producer's active or relevant alarms. It works in two directions: asynchronous notification, where the producer sends a fault notification to the MnS consumer when the alarm occurs, when the severity changes and when the alarm is removed; and query/control, where the MnS consumer reads the alarm list with or without a filter and works with optional history mechanisms.

conceitos.t: The fault notifications, one by one
conceitos.d: Slide 30 separates what a producer sends from what it should send. It sends: notifyNewAlarm (a new alarm has appeared), notifyChangedAlarmGeneral (some attribute of an existing alarm changed, for example severity or text), notifyClearedAlarm (the fault condition no longer exists) and notifyAlarmListRebuilt (the alarm list was rebuilt). It should support: notifyAckStateChanged (a change in the alarm's acknowledgement state, if the NF supports acknowledgment) and notifyPotentialFaultyAlarmList (the alarm list may not be up to date; it can happen between locked/disabled and the rebuild — in that case the producer must flag the situation and must not send 3GPP fault supervision notifications). The difference between 'shall' and 'should' matters when assessing a piece of equipment: the first four are the minimum, the last two are recommended.

conceitos.t: Performance Assurance: what to measure and how often
conceitos.d: The O1 interface service responsible for collecting and making NF performance data available to the SMO, and which lets the SMO determine what to measure and how often to report. There are two operation families. Reporting: file-based (batch) or continuous streaming. Control: definition of which metrics to report, definition of reporting frequency/period and control of measurement processes. File-based reporting has two modes. Pull-based: the file becomes ready at the producer, the producer signals that the file is ready and the consumer retrieves the file. Push-based: the producer transfers the file to the consumer or to a designated server, signals that it is ready and sent, and the consumer retrieves the file from the predetermined location. In continuous streaming the producer establishes a continuous connection and streams data to the consumer. Control is done through a metric collection/reporting object of type PerfMetricJob IOC, created and controlled by the consumer, which defines the desired measurements, periodicity, delivery mechanism, file location and filters.

The O1 interface service responsible for tracing the behavior of the NFs and defining methods for recording that information so the cause and effect of events can be understood. The deck details four collection types. Call Trace: session/call/connection tracing — how the session was established, which signalling messages occurred, whether there was an anomaly point and the behavior of the UE and the network throughout the session; used for troubleshooting a specific UE, investigating intermittent failures, signalling analysis and mobility/session analysis. MDT (Minimization of Drive Testing): uses the UEs and the network behavior to assess network coverage and quality, with two methods — immediate, where measurements are reported close to the event, and logged, where they are stored and can be retrieved later; it serves coverage optimization, handover tuning, cell-edge analysis and post-deployment validation. And two from the RRC domain (Radio Resource Control, the layer/protocol responsible for controlling establishment, configuration, measurements, mobility and release of the connection between the UE and the radio network): RCEF (RRC Connection Establishment Failure), when a failure occurs in the UE's connection process with the network, and RLF (Radio Link Failure), when a failure occurs in the UE's connection process with the radio. RRC reporting is the set of reports with event diagnostics and RRC-domain information generated by the UE and retrieved by the gNB.

conceitos.t: Trace Management: TraceJob, activation and delivery
conceitos.d: The general tracing steps are six: create/configure a TraceJob, activate the Trace Session, wait for the trigger event, the producer generates trace records, the data is delivered to the consumer and the session is closed. There are two activation methods. Management-based: done through management, with the SMO sending a command over the O1 interface, configuring the TraceJob, and the session being activated/deactivated by management mechanisms. Signalling-based: done from commands received through signalling messages. And two data delivery methods: file-based tracing, where records are collected into files and delivered to the consumer with some delay, and streaming-based tracing, where data is sent in bursts over a WebSocket connection. Control is a management object of type TraceJob IOC, which defines trace type, delivery mode, data destination, selection conditions, job state and triggers. The data model is the usual one — YANG to model the TraceJob, NETCONF for the CRUD operations, REST/HTTP + JSON for notifications — plus WebSocket, which only shows up here, in streaming-based tracing.

conceitos.t: File Management: discovering, listing and transferring files
conceitos.d: The O1 interface service responsible for delivering or fetching file artifacts generated by other services and for letting the SMO discover, query and transfer them. It does not produce the files: it carries what the other services produced — data generated by file-based tracing, management measurement reports and performance measurements, software files, beamforming configuration files, machine learning artifacts and certificates. There are three operations. File Ready Notification, to tell the consumer that a file is available for retrieval: a new file is available at the producer, the producer sends notifyFileReady to the consumer, mutual certificate authentication takes place and the transfer starts over HTTP/TLS. List Available Files, where the consumer queries the producer to learn which files are available: it receives the list of files and locations and decides whether to download, ignore or trigger another process. File Transfer/Download, to transfer files securely: the consumer establishes a NETCONF session with the producer, sends a NETCONF RPC file-download with the file location, the producer answers whether it can start the download, the NETCONF session is closed and the producer establishes a secure connection to perform the download over SFTP, FTPeS or HTTPS.

conceitos.t: PNF Software Management: from inventory to fallback
conceitos.d: The O1 interface service responsible for end-to-end software management of physical network functions, from inventory and download to activation and recovery. The software lifecycle is: download a package, install, validate and activate; the inventory/version control says which packages exist, which are active or passive and which version is available. The service exports an object of type softwarePackage with package name, version, file list, integrity status (valid, invalid or empty), execution state (active, the software currently running; passive, software already loaded on the equipment but not yet active), vendor, product name and software type (operational or factory, the factory image used as a last-resort recovery). The operation has four pieces: software inventory, which lets the consumer check which software packages exist on the PNF before any upgrade (active version, passive version, whether there is a factory image and which packages exist); software download, where the consumer asks the producer to download the needed files from a software server; integrity verification, with checksum, hardware compatibility and package consistency; and software activation pre-check, which verifies activation in progress, IntegrityStatus in a valid state and compatibility between software and platform. Resilience has three mechanisms: restart, which activation may require for correct operation; data migration, when the new version requires changing the internal database, persistent files or configuration structures; and fallback/rollback, which on an activation failure tries to return to the previously active software and, if that also fails, to the factory software. On package naming and content the deck is explicit: the service defines the management process, but the PNF has autonomy to define the format of its own packages and which ones are needed for operation.

conceitos.t: The repeating pattern: YANG models, NETCONF operates, REST/HTTP notifies
conceitos.d: The six services barely vary in their data model, and noticing that saves a lot of memorizing. YANG models the data: it defines which objects exist, which attributes they have, and types, constraints and structure — it is the schema of what can be read and written, and it opens step 1 of almost every flow in the deck. NETCONF runs the operations: it is through get, get-config and edit-config that the SMO reads the cell configuration, creates a PerfMetricJob, creates and activates a TraceJob, reads the AlarmList or triggers a file-download. REST/HTTP + JSON delivers the notifications, always from producer to consumer: notifyConfigDataChange, notifyNewAlarm, notifyChangedAlarmGeneral, notifyClearedAlarm, notifyFileReady, notifyTraceFileReady. Two exceptions show up: WebSocket, used only in streaming-based tracing, and SFTP, FTPeS or HTTPS, used for the actual transport of files and software packages. In one sentence: the command goes over NETCONF, the heads-up comes over REST/HTTP, and the heavy file comes over the transfer protocols.

conceitos.t: The six services in the closing table
conceitos.d: Slide 70 closes the lesson with the six services by focus, typical actions and typical timing. Provisioning Management Services: focus on the configuration of the NF and of the managed objects; creates, changes, removes and reads configuration and receives config change; at deployment, initial parameterization and reconfiguration. Fault Supervision Management Services: fault and alarm supervision; receives alarms, queries the alarm list, filters alarms and follows severity/clear; in continuous operation, troubleshooting and incidents. Performance Assurance Management Services: collection and delivery of performance metrics; creates measurement jobs, chooses metrics, sets periodicity and receives PM files/streaming; in continuous operation, optimization and capacity planning. Trace Management Services: detailed session/event/UE-oriented observation; creates a TraceJob, activates/deactivates the trace and collects trace file/streaming; in deep troubleshooting, UE analysis and investigation of specific events. File Management Services: file discovery and transfer; lists files, receives notifyFileReady, requests transfers and downloads files; in operational support, artifact collection and file delivery/retrieval. PNF Software Management Services: software upgrade cycle for physical functions; software inventory, download, validation, activation, reset and fallback; in maintenance, upgrade, version fixes and planned updates.

onde.texto: In our lab O1 really exists: the SDN-R/OpenDaylight controller speaks NETCONF/TLS to the simulated O-DU (pynts) and the panel reaches it over RESTCONF. Provisioning shows up in four tests: smo-o1-leitura does the read side (get and get-config over the 3GPP models of the gNB-DU and the NR cell the O-DU advertises); smo-o1-prov does the write cycle of slide 25 — it reads gNBDUName, writes it with edit-config, checks it inside the equipment itself and undoes it; smo-p2-prov applies a network plan in bulk to the managed functions; and smo-p2-escala does the full CRUD of slide 21 on a brand-new NRCellDU cell: create, read, change and delete. Fault Supervision shows up in smo-falhas and smo-p2-operacao, with a difference worth stating: the alarm travels as a VES event to the Kafka topic, not as an AlarmRecord read over NETCONF from the AlarmList of slide 33 — the simulated O-DU ships no alarm recipe, so the test plays the element's part, in the VES 7.2.1 format it would use. Performance Assurance and File Management come together in smo-telemetria: the O-DU writes the 3GPP measurement file, announces it with VES FileReady and the SMO fetches the file — it is the notifyFileReady of slides 42 and 59 in pull mode, but without the SMO creating a PerfMetricJob over O1; the periodicity comes from the element's own configuration, not from a job the SMO asked for. Trace Management has no test: no element in the lab exposes a TraceJob. PNF Software Management has none either; the closest is smo-ciclo-vida, which terminates and reinstantiates a network function and measures the call home — that is container lifecycle, the role that would belong to O2, not the O1 softwarePackage. And smo-p2-pilha shows what comes before everything: the three functions instantiated and how long the SMO takes to bring each one under management, with nobody configuring the controller.

quiz.q: Worked example — Scenario: an O-DU being managed by the SMO over O1. The components are one SMO, one O-DU, a management function associated with that O-DU and the O1 interface between them; the operator wants to configure O-DU parameters, collect performance metrics and receive alarms. Who is the NF? Who is the set of one or more NFs? Who is the NE's equivalent in the management context? Who is the NF's equivalent in the management context? What are the Provisioning, Fault Supervision, Performance Assurance and Software Management services called? And what is the set of MnS called?
quiz.a: The slide 8 answers, in order: the NF is the O-DU; the set of one or more NFs is the Network Element (NE); the NE's equivalent in the management context is the ManagedElement; the NF's equivalent in the management context is the ManagedFunction; the services are the Management Service (MnS); and the set of MnS is the Management Function (MnF). The slide 5 drawing nails it down: on top, the operation view, with O-DU (NF) and O-CU (NF) inside the Network Element (NE); below, the management view, with the O-DU ManagedFunction and the O-CU ManagedFunction inside the Managed Element (ME), the MnS blocks grouped in the MnF, the SMO behind the MnS Consumer block and the managed side behind the MnS Producer block.

quiz.q: Same scenario, Case 1 — configuration: the operator wants to change a cell parameter on the O-DU. Who does what, and in what order?
quiz.a: The five steps of slide 9: 1) the SMO acts as MnS Consumer; 2) it uses the provisioning MnS; 3) that service is exposed by the MnF; 4) the MnF applies the change to the ManagedFunction corresponding to the O-DU; 5) the effective configuration changes the NF's behavior. Notice the path: the SMO never touches the O-DU directly. It calls a service, the service is exposed by a management function, the management function writes to the O-DU's representative (the ManagedFunction) and only then does the equipment change behavior. That is exactly why the four names on slide 3 exist.

quiz.q: Same scenario, Case 2 — fault: the O-DU detects an anomalous condition. What happens, and in what order?
quiz.a: The five steps of slide 9: 1) the MnF generates a notification in the fault supervision MnS; 2) it acts as MnS Producer; 3) the SMO receives the notification as MnS Consumer; 4) the SMO correlates the event with other network information; 5) the operator or the automation makes a decision. Compare with Case 1: in provisioning the SMO speaks first and the MnF executes; in a fault the MnF speaks first and the SMO receives. The roles do not change owners — the service producer is still the managed side and the consumer is still the SMO — what changes is who starts the conversation.

quiz.q: A user is making a call. Does that call's traffic go through O1?
quiz.a: No. Slide 12 asks the question on its own and slide 13 closes the answer: O1 does not carry user traffic but management information. The call's traffic runs on the RAN user and control planes; only the six management services go over O1 — Provisioning, Fault Supervision, Performance Assurance, Trace, Files and PNF Software — with the MnS Consumer usually being the SMO and the MnS Producer being the managed side, the NF's management function.

quiz.q: Provisioning flow — Scenario: the operator deployed an O-DU and needs to parameterize it. Walk through the three stages, saying which operation shows up at each step.
quiz.a: Stage 1, modelling (slide 23): the YANG model defines which objects exist, which attributes they have, and types, constraints and structure. Stage 2, operation (slides 24 to 26): 1) the SMO identifies the available NF; 2) it opens a NETCONF session with the producer; 3) it issues a NETCONF get-config request to read the current configuration — in the example, an rpc get-config on the running datastore with a subtree filter over urn:o-ran:cell-config:1.0, and the reply brings cellId CELL-001, administrativeState LOCKED, pci 100 and arfcn 635334; 5) it locks the datastore; 6) it uses edit-config to apply the new parameters — in the example, administrativeState goes to UNLOCKED and pci from 100 to 120; 7) it uses get or get-config to verify the result; 8) it receives the producer's reply (an rpc-reply with ok); 9) it uses unlock to release the datastore; 10) it closes the session with close-session. Stage 3, event (slide 27): the producer sends a notification over REST/HTTP with a JSON payload — 1) the producer sends it by HTTP POST to /o1/notifications/configuration-change; 2) the notification body comes in JSON, with notificationType notifyConfigDataChange and the changedAttributes list carrying oldValue and newValue of each attribute; 3) the SMO updates its configuration view. A note on the numbering: the deck jumps from step 3 to step 5 — there is no step 4 in the slides. By the sequence, what is missing is the get-config reply, which is drawn alongside on slide 24.

quiz.q: Alarm flow — Scenario: an O-DU loses transport connectivity. Walk through the flow from the YANG model to the alarm leaving the list.
quiz.a: Stage 1, modelling (slide 31): the YANG model defines the alarm list and the alarm record, with id, affected resource, probable cause, severity, state, time and additional text. Stage 2, information consumption (slides 32 and 33): 1) the MnF detects the fault; 2) an AlarmRecord is created/updated; 3) the alarm is registered in the AlarmList; 4) notifyNewAlarm is sent to the SMO — an HTTP POST to /o1/notifications/fault with alarmId ALM-0001, resource ManagedFunction=O-DU-01, probableCause 'Transport link failure', perceivedSeverity MAJOR and alarmState ACTIVE; 5) the SMO receives it and correlates; 6) the SMO does a get over NETCONF on the AlarmList to validate the current state; 7) and then issues a NETCONF get-config request to read the current configuration. The story continues on slide 34, which restarts the numbering at 6 (repeating the previous slide's numbers): the fault worsens and the producer sends a notification signalling the severity change — notifyChangedAlarmGeneral, with perceivedSeverity rising from MAJOR to CRITICAL; the link comes back and the producer sends an alarm-clear notification — notifyClearedAlarm, with perceivedSeverity and alarmState as CLEARED; and the alarm is removed from the AlarmList once it is no longer active. Notice the pair of directions: the producer pushes the three notifications (new, changed, cleared) and the SMO pulls the AlarmList over NETCONF to check for itself.

quiz.q: Slide 37 quiz: the metrics file is ready. Who starts the transfer? A) SMO; B) Producer; C) It depends on the mechanism.
quiz.a: Option C — it depends on the mechanism. Slide 38 marks C and explains it with the two cases. Pull: the producer signals and the SMO retrieves. Push: the producer transfers, the producer signals and the SMO retrieves. In other words, the one who announces is always the producer; what changes is whether the file has already been moved to the destination (push) or is still at the producer waiting to be fetched (pull). And note that in both cases slide 36 ends the same way, with 'the consumer retrieves the file' — in push, from the predetermined location.

quiz.q: Measurement flow — Scenario: creating measurement jobs. Walk through the stages and say which reporting mode this flow uses.
quiz.a: Stage 1, modelling (slide 39): the YANG model defines a measurement job with identifier, administrative state, reporting method, periodicity, file location and desired metric group. Stage 2, creating the job (slides 40 to 42): 1) the SMO requests the creation of a PerfMetricJob over NETCONF following the YANG model — in the example, an edit-config over urn:o-ran:performance-assurance:1.0 with job-id PMJOB-001, administrative-state UNLOCKED, reporting-method FILE_PULL, reporting-period-sec 300, file-location at the producer and target-measurement-group OR.CellPerformance; 2) metric collection starts happening according to the requirements — and slide 41 shows the query (a get filtering by job-id PMJOB-001) with the reply carrying the already created job; 3) the producer sends notifyFileReady over REST/HTTP to the SMO — a POST to /o1/notifications/performance with fileInfo containing fileName, fileLocation and reportingMethod FILE_PULL; 4) the SMO uses the fileLocation to fetch the file and process the metrics. The mode is the pull of the slide 37 quiz: reporting-method FILE_PULL, the producer signals, the SMO retrieves. A deck detail: the slides of this flow still carry the title 'Alarm flow', inherited from the previous service — the scenario is about measurement.

quiz.q: Trace flow — Scenario: the SMO wants to create a file-based Call Trace for a given UE. Walk through the five stages.
quiz.a: Stage 1, modelling (slide 49): the YANG model defines trace type, state, delivery form, destination, trigger and target UE, when applicable. Stage 2, creation (slide 50): the SMO requests the creation of a TraceJob over NETCONF following the YANG model. Stage 3, activation (slide 51): the SMO activates the job, changing the state to ACTIVATED over NETCONF — in the example, an edit-config over urn:o-ran:trace-management:1.0 with job-id TRACE-001 and activation-state ACTIVATED — and collection starts happening according to the requirements. Stage 4, query (slide 52): the NF detects the RRC_SETUP_COMPLETE trigger, collection happens according to the requirements and the producer creates trace records; the get reply shows the job with job-type CALL_TRACE, delivery-mode FILE, file-location, trigger-condition RRC_SETUP_COMPLETE and target-ue-id UE-12345. Stage 5, delivery (slide 53): the producer generates a periodic file and announces it — a POST to /o1/notifications/trace with notificationType notifyTraceFileReady and traceFileInfo carrying fileName, fileLocation and deliveryMode FILE. Compare with the general steps of slide 47 — create/configure the TraceJob, activate the Trace Session, wait for the trigger, generate trace records, deliver to the consumer and close the session: closing is the only step the drawn flow does not show.

quiz.q: File flow — Scenario: the SMO wants to retrieve files with trace information. Walk through the four stages.
quiz.a: Stage 1, modelling (slide 58): the YANG model defines the management objects of the file service, with two data blocks — available-files, the files already available at the producer, and file-download-requests, the requests for the producer to download a file from somewhere else. Stage 2, notification (slide 59): the producer generates a trace file and tells the SMO, sending notifyFileReady over REST/HTTP with TLS protection and a JSON payload — in the example, a POST to /o1/notifications/file-management with fileInfo containing fileName, fileType TRACE_DATA, fileLocation, fileFormat application/octet-stream and fileSizeBytes. Stage 3 (slide 60 repeats the label 'Notification', but the content is the listing): the SMO lists the available files — a NETCONF get with a subtree filter over available-files in urn:o-ran:file-management:1.0, and the reply brings each file-entry with name, type, location, format and size. Stage 4, transfer (slide 61): the file is transferred using the HTTPS or SFTP or FTPeS file transfer protocol — in the example, a GET to /files/<file> with an Authorization Bearer header. Both paths of slide 55 appear together here: the producer announces (File Ready Notification) and the consumer can also ask (List Available Files).

quiz.q: Upgrade flow — Scenario: the operator wants to upgrade the software of a PNF. Walk through the six stages.
quiz.a: Stage 1, inventory query / modelling (slide 66): the YANG model defines an object of type software-package for the download and activate operations, with the important fields integrity (valid, invalid or empty), state (active or passive) and software type (operational or factory). Stage 2, inventory query (slide 67): the SMO needs to know the packages' situation (active or passive) and their integrity, and finds that oru-sw-A is active, oru-sw-B is passive but still empty, and that a factory image exists. Stage 3, software download (slide 67): the SMO wants the PNF to download the new oru-sw-B version from an external server, and NETCONF points to where the producer should fetch the package and associate it with the oru-sw-B package. Stage 4, software download (slide 68): it opens a secure connection; downloads the package, and if the download takes long the producer may send periodic status; understands the vendor-specific format; extracts the files it needs; runs the integrity verification; saves to a persistent location; and updates the inventory. Stage 5, software activation pre-check (slide 69): check for an activation in progress, check that the package state is passive, the integrity state and the compatibility between software and hardware. Stage 6, software activation (slide 69): it makes oru-sw-B the active package; it may run data migration steps and a PNF restart, complete or perform fallback/rollback; and it updates the inventory with the state change. Watch the titles: stages 1 and 2 have the same name in the deck ('Inventory query') and so do stages 3 and 4 ('Software download') — slide 66 is the modelling, 67 brings the inventory and the download request, and 68 brings the download itself.

quiz.q: Built from the slide 70 table: which of the six Management Services do you use in each case? A) change the PCI of a freshly deployed cell; B) see the filtered list of active alarms after an incident; C) receive per-cell throughput every 5 minutes; D) a specific UE cannot connect and you want to see its signalling; E) the producer announced a file is ready and you want to download it; F) roll out a new firmware version on an O-RU.
quiz.a: A) Provisioning Management Services — focus on the configuration of the NF and of the managed objects; typical timing: deployment, initial parameterization, reconfiguration. B) Fault Supervision Management Services — receive alarms, query the alarm list, filter alarms and follow severity/clear; typical timing: continuous operation, troubleshooting, incidents. C) Performance Assurance Management Services — create measurement jobs, choose metrics, set periodicity and receive PM files/streaming; it is the PerfMetricJob of slide 36. D) Trace Management Services — detailed session/event/UE-oriented observation, with a TraceJob and trace file/streaming collection; it is the Call Trace of slide 43. E) File Management Services — list files, receive notifyFileReady, request transfers and download files. F) PNF Software Management Services — software inventory, download, validation, activation, reset and fallback. Mind the C–E and D–E boundaries: Performance Assurance decides what to measure and Trace decides what to trace, but the one that moves the file is always File Management.
